checkpoints: A full-history join re-walked on every call makes cost scale with total ledger size rather than with how much activity happened between requests — a dashboard polling this endpoint every few seconds re-fetches and re-sums every intent's refunds from scratch even though only a handful of payments and refunds occurred since the previous poll.

Maintaining a per-intent totalRefunded as a stored running counter, updated in the same write path that flips a refund to Succeeded, replaces an O(intents x refunds) re-filter-and-reduce with a simple field read; keeping the counter rebuildable from the ledger via a periodic reconciliation job means a bug in the counter self-heals instead of becoming a silent, permanent lie in the report.

Caching the whole report as a versioned snapshot and invalidating it the instant a payment or refund write lands turns repeated full joins into a single reused computation, trading a few seconds of staleness for eliminating redundant work — an acceptable trade because the consumer is a dashboard poll, not a strict real-time feed.

Scoping the report by settlement period narrows the initial payment scan to one window instead of the entire ledger's history, since reconciliation is naturally periodic work and its cost should track the period being reconciled rather than the full lifetime of the ledger.

Across every optimization strategy, totalRefunded must keep counting only refunds with status Succeeded and every monetary sum must stay in integer cents with no floating-point rounding introduced — these correctness constraints cannot be relaxed just because the computation path changed.

ReconciliationService has to remain strictly read-only no matter how it's optimized; none of incremental aggregates, caching, or period scoping should turn it into a place that writes a corrected netAmount or any other figure back onto a payment record.

Because this report serves a periodic audit dashboard rather than a real-time feed, trading a bounded amount of staleness for much less repeated work — via caching or period scoping — is the right default, and full incremental real-time accuracy is only worth reaching for when a consumer genuinely can't tolerate any staleness.

Validating the optimization means running the new path against the original brute-force join over an identical ledger, including a mix of failed refunds to confirm they stay excluded, and checking that both per-line and aggregate netAmount match exactly before load-testing at the dashboard's real polling interval to confirm the latency improvement is real.
